summary: Switch diagnostics means using show commands and counters to locate problems quickly: link state, MAC learning, VLANs, trunks, spanning tree, and bundles. Work from the physical layer upward.

sections.heading: A systematic approach
bullets: Layer 1: is the link up, at the right speed and duplex, with clean counters?
Layer 2: are MACs learned, is the port in the right VLAN, is the trunk allowing it, is spanning tree forwarding?
Layer 3: do the host and gateway share the subnet, and is the ARP entry present?
Change one thing at a time and re-test.

sections.heading: Core show commands (Cisco IOS style)
bullets: show interfaces status: port up/down, VLAN, duplex, speed at a glance.
show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1: detailed counters.
show mac address-table [address|interface|vlan]: where a device was learned.
show vlan brief: VLANs and their access ports.
show interfaces trunk: trunk ports, allowed and active VLANs, native VLAN.
show spanning-tree [vlan N]: root bridge, port roles and states.
show etherchannel summary: bundle membership and flags.
show cdp neighbors / show lldp neighbors: what is attached to each port.
show logging: link flaps, MAC flapping, err-disable events.

sections.heading: Reading interface counters
bullets: CRC / input errors: bad cable, interference, duplex mismatch.
Runts and giants: collisions or MTU mismatch.
Output drops: congestion.
Late collisions: duplex mismatch or too-long cabling.
Resets/flaps: unstable link or failing optic.

sections.heading: Common symptoms and checks
bullets: Port down/down: cable, remote end, or err-disabled (check `show interfaces status err-disabled`).
Link up, no traffic: wrong VLAN, trunk not allowing the VLAN, or port security violation.
Slow link: speed/duplex mismatch or errors.
Intermittent: loops (STP), MAC flapping, or a failing cable.
Host cannot reach gateway: ARP, VLAN, or default gateway misconfiguration.

subtopics.title: Linux equivalents
subtopics.summary: Same questions on a host or bridge.

sections.body: `ip -s link` shows counters and errors; `ethtool eth0` shows speed and duplex; `bridge fdb show` is the MAC table; `bridge vlan show` lists VLANs; `ip neigh` is ARP.
sections.code:
$ ethtool eth0 | grep -E 'Speed|Duplex|Link'
$ ip -s link show eth0

subtopics.title: Packet captures
subtopics.summary: See what is on the wire.

sections.body: SPAN/port mirroring copies traffic to an analyzer port; Wireshark or tcpdump then shows ARP, STP BPDUs, and LACPDUs directly. Filter on `arp`, `stp`, or `ether proto 0x8809`.

Symptoms: very high CPU, utilization near 100%, rapidly increasing broadcast counters, MAC flapping logs. Find the looping ports from the interface with the fastest-growing counters, shut one, and fix the topology or enable BPDU guard.

Ports shut themselves down on BPDU guard, port security, or link flap events. `show interfaces status err-disabled` names the cause; fix it, then `shutdown` / `no shutdown` (or configure auto-recovery).
Keep configuration backups, a port map, and baseline counters so deviations are obvious. Use SNMP or streaming telemetry to alert on error and utilization trends.

takeaways: Troubleshoot bottom-up: link, MAC/VLAN/trunk, STP, then IP.
Know the key commands: interfaces status, mac address-table, vlan brief, trunk, spanning-tree, etherchannel.
Counters tell the story: CRC means cabling, runts/giants mean MTU or collisions, drops mean congestion.
Loops show as broadcast storms and MAC flapping.
